verifications.claim: The 25th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution was ratified in 1967.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'Ratified in 1967'; R2: 'The states completed ratification by February 10, 1967'; R4: 'Ratified February 10, 1967'; R5: 'ratified in 1967'; R6: 'ratified on February 10, 1967'; R7: 'ratified by the states on June 10, 1967'
verifications.reasoning: Multiple sources directly state ratification in 1967.

verifications.claim: Section 1 of the 25th Amendment explicitly states that if the President dies, resigns, or is removed, the Vice President becomes President.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'Section 1 ... provides that if the President dies, resigns, or is removed from office ... the Vice President "shall become President."'; R4, R6, R7 quote Section 1 identically.
verifications.reasoning: Direct quotes of Section 1 in multiple sources match the claim exactly.

verifications.claim: Section 2 of the 25th Amendment allows the President to nominate a Vice President if a vacancy occurs, subject to congressional approval.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'Section 2 ... requires the President to nominate a new Vice President ... after confirmation by a majority vote in each chamber of Congress'; R4, R6, R7 quote Section 2 identically.
verifications.reasoning: Direct quotes and descriptions match precisely.

verifications.claim: Section 3 of the 25th Amendment allows the President to temporarily transfer power to the Vice President (Acting President) if they cannot fulfill duties.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'Section 3 allows an incapacitated President ... to relinquish his powers and duties voluntarily ... the Vice President serves as Acting President'; R4, R6, R7 quote Section 3 identically.
verifications.reasoning: Direct quotes and explanations confirm temporary transfer to Acting President.

verifications.claim: Section 4 of the 25th Amendment empowers the Vice President and a majority of the Cabinet to declare the President incapacitated and remove them from power.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'Section 4 ... allows the Vice President and a majority of the "principal officers of the executive departments" ... to initiate the transfer'; R3: 'Section 4 ... allows the vice president and a majority of cabinet secretaries to remove the president'; R4, R5, R6, R7 quote Section 4.
verifications.reasoning: Sources describe VP and Cabinet declaring incapacity, leading to transfer of power.

verifications.claim: An article from Congress.gov notes that Section 1 was used in 1974 when Gerald Ford became president following Richard Nixon's resignation.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'In 1974, Section 1 resulted in Vice President Gerald Ford's succession to the presidency when President Richard Nixon resigned'; R6: similar description.
verifications.reasoning: Congress.gov sources (R1, R6) directly note the 1974 use of Section 1.

verifications.claim: Section 3 has been used multiple times.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'a few Presidents have invoked Section 3'; R7: Reagan (1985), Bush (twice), Biden.
verifications.reasoning: 'A few' and specific multiple instances confirm more than once.

verifications.claim: Section 3 has been used during presidential surgeries.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'temporarily while undergoing medical procedures'; R3: 'when presidents are undergoing health procedures'; R7: Reagan surgery, Bush medical procedures.
verifications.reasoning: Sources explicitly link Section 3 invocations to surgeries/medical procedures.

verifications.claim: Section 4 has never been invoked to permanently remove a president, according to Newsweek.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R5 (Newsweek): 'never successfully used to permanently remove a president'; R1: 'Section 4, which has never been invoked'.
verifications.reasoning: Newsweek (R5) directly states it has never been used to permanently remove.

verifications.claim: Section 4 requires a two-thirds vote in both houses of Congress if the president contests it, according to Newsweek.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R5 (Newsweek): 'two-thirds majorities in both the House and Senate would be required to uphold the removal'; R4, R6, R7 quote Section 4 text.
verifications.reasoning: Newsweek and Section 4 quotes confirm two-thirds vote requirement.

verifications.claim: The 25th Amendment was created to address ambiguities regarding presidential disability, particularly following the assassination of President John F. Kennedy, according to the Gerald R. Ford Presidential Library & Museum.
verifications.label: INCORRECT
verifications.evidence: R2 (Ford Library): 'rules of succession to the Presidency were constitutionally vague ... clarifying and defining the rules on Presidential succession and inability' (no mention of JFK); R7: 'Following President John F. Kennedy’s assassination ... prompted Congress to address questions'.
verifications.reasoning: R2 (Ford Library) supports addressing ambiguities but does not mention JFK assassination; claim incorrectly attributes 'particularly following JFK' to R2.
